articles.title: Do Palestinians in Gaza expect anything to change after Israel’s election?
articles.summary: After years of war, displacement and restrictions, Gazans ask whether Israel’s election will affect their future.
articles.body:
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip — After three years of genocidal war, Palestinians in Gaza are watching the upcoming elections in Israel with a mixture of fear and uncertainty.

Although the territory has been under a “ceasefire” since October 2025, Palestinians in Gaza continue to endure almost daily Israeli air strikes, dire living conditions, and a punishing siege that has caused shortages of basic goods.

Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday to vote for their next government, in an election that has been shaped by the war on Gaza. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been strongly criticised for his handling of security before the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel. Members of his far-right government have called for a tougher line on Gaza, including the expulsion of its population.

The people of Gaza know this election will shape their future and many have been closely watching the campaign.

Mohammed Eliyan, 36, was displaced from Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza and now lives in Deir el-Balah with his five children. He hopes a change in leadership in Israel could bring relief to Palestinians who have endured repeated displacement and war.

“We follow the Israeli election to see who will win in the next phase. We hope there might be some easing for the Palestinian cause and for us, who have been displaced again,” he told Al Jazeera.

Eliyan hopes that Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military commander and Netanyahu’s main rival, will defeat the prime minister. He sees Netanyahu as more hardline and fears that if his Likud party and far-right allies win another term, it would mean more war and further displacement for Gaza’s people.

“We hope there will be changes after the election, and that someone other than Benjamin Netanyahu will win. What Netanyahu has done to the Palestinian people, before and after October 7, has not been a small thing,” he said.

But regardless of who wins, Eliyan does not expect a major shift in Israeli policy.

“They are still our enemy, and I don’t expect things to improve dramatically,” he said. “But we hope someone else might be less harsh than Netanyahu.”

He called on Israel’s next leader to end the war, prevent displacement and starvation, and ease restrictions at Gaza’s crossings.

“We want whoever leads Israel not to be hardline. End the war and let us live in peace,” he said.

Islam Salem, 41, is displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and has three daughters. He is following Israel’s election closely and believes the result could affect Gaza’s future and the lives of his children, likely for the worse.

“Politics is our livelihood. It is connected to everything in our lives, our living conditions and even the future of our children,” he said.

But he also believes that elections primarily serve Israeli interests, so even if there are new faces in the next government, the Gaza strategy will likely remain the same.

“Israeli policy will not change in any way. Whatever they take, they consider it theirs and a political gain for them, the gains of a war they have pursued for a long time,” Islam told Al Jazeera.

He pointed to Israel’s continued control of about 65 percent of Gaza’s territory inside the “Yellow Line”. He also doubts whether reconstruction will begin soon in Gaza, where more than 80 percent of buildings have been damaged, and about two-thirds of those have been completely destroyed.

“I think reconstruction will be difficult. They do not want to give others any rights. They want their rights in full, and even more,” he said.

Years of war have left Salem struggling to imagine a future beyond his harsh daily reality.

“There is no future left for us to be afraid of. We live day by day. We have no idea what will happen next, and everything we feared has already happened,” he said.

Asked what he would say to Israel’s next prime minister, he spoke of how many in Gaza are feeling.

“If only a simple person could come and talk to him and say, ‘Leave us alone. Give us some breathing space and let us breathe.’ But he would not be convinced. What can I say to him?” he said.

Hanan Abu al-Maaza, 57, has been displaced more than 12 times during the war on Gaza. She fears Israel’s next government could bring more suffering to its people in the besieged enclave.

“We follow the election because of the fear and anxiety we are living with. We have been displaced more than 12 times, and we are afraid they will do even worse to us than before,” she said.

“We go to sleep without feeling safe, wondering what they might do to us next. The fear is still in our heads and hearts.”

Abu al-Maaza says if Netanyahu is defeated, there will be more chance that she can return to her home in Beit Lahiya.

“I hope someone else wins, so we can have peace of mind and feel safe, and return to our homes. That is what we wish for,” she said.

After years of destruction in Gaza, she hopes Israel’s next leader will show Palestinians more mercy.

“Maybe he will say that there is nothing left in Gaza, that they have done enough and should let people live. There is hardly anything left in Gaza for anyone to think about doing anything more,” she said.

Abu al-Maaza urged Israel’s next leader to end the war and stop the suffering in the territory.

“We have had enough of war and destruction. There is nothing left to destroy, yet the suffering continues,” she said.

Manar Owaida, 23, is originally from northern Gaza and is now displaced in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City. She is also keeping an eye on the Israeli election and considering its potential impact.

“I follow the election to know what they are saying and planning, and to understand what is happening around us and how the next Israeli government might affect the situation in Gaza,” she said.

Owaida hopes Gadi Eisenkot will replace Netanyahu, and sees the current prime minister as more extreme than his challenger. But she does not believe a change in Israel’s leadership would transform Palestinian lives, arguing that government policies have remained consistent for decades.

“Israel’s policy is one of crime, killing and destruction. Since 1948, it has been the same policy, the same killing and the same blockade,” she said.

Still, she hopes a new government could ease restrictions and killings and withdraw from areas beyond the “Yellow Line”, allowing life to gradually return to Gaza.

“There might be a change in Israeli policy if someone comes in place of Netanyahu and eases the blockade and the killing we are living through,” she said.

“There could be a withdrawal from the Yellow Line and life could gradually return to Gaza. But we are waiting with fear and uncertainty, alongside a little hope.”

Her greatest concern is that Netanyahu could launch a wider regional war to avoid domestic political pressure around the time of the vote.

Owaida said she wants Israel’s next prime minister to allow Palestinians to live without fear of further violence.

“We want to live in freedom and peace, away from killing and wars,” she said.

Mousa Ali, 33, was displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and is now in Gaza City with his four children.

He believes that the outcome of the election could determine whether displaced Palestinians can return to areas beyond the “Yellow Line”.

“For Palestinians, this election is critical, especially because of the Yellow Line. We hope the opposition will be better when it comes to allowing displaced people to return to their areas,” he said.

Ali mentioned Gadi Eisenkot as a possible alternative and hopes Arab parties will perform strongly so they have a role in the next government.

But he does not expect a new leader to bring major changes for the people of Gaza and fears that Israeli attacks will continue. He says a Netanyahu victory would prolong displacement and control over areas around the “Yellow Line”.

“Every day in Gaza, there is blood, there are people being killed, and there is bombing everywhere,” he said. “We hope this policy will end and that a new prime minister will stop this ongoing bloodshed.”

articles.title: Meet Sophia Fan, the 17-year-old Maryland student who found forgotten books under her stairs and turned the idea into a nonprofit that has distributed more than 7,000 books in four years across the US and abroad
articles.summary: Nobody would have thought that a forgotten cupboard of books under the stairs would give someone an idea that would eventually reach thousands of children
articles.body: Nobody would have thought that a forgotten cupboard of books under the stairs would give someone an idea that would eventually reach thousands of children in the United States and other countries. The 17-year-old student from Urbana, Maryland, Sophia Fan, started collecting and redistributing used books when she was just 13, and her initiative, Literacy Cycle, has now donated more than 7,000 books in just four years.What began with books that were no longer in use has grown into a nonprofit that collects Advanced Placement (AP) textbooks, SAT preparation materials and children’s books for young people who may not have easy access to them. According to PEOPLE, Literacy Cycle has expanded beyond Maryland, with chapters in five other US states and an international chapter in Rwanda.How a cupboard full of old books inspired the initiativeFan, now a senior at Urbana High School, had been surrounded by books since childhood. One of her early favourites was a My Little Pony book that she remembers taking her into another world. Years later, while sorting through books she had outgrown, she came across a collection that had been left unused and began thinking about how the stories and learning materials could reach and help other children as well.In an interview with PEOPLE, Fan recalled finding the cupboard under the stairs filled with books she had used as a child, including stories she had forgotten about. Rather than leaving them there, she wanted to share them with students who could make use of them.The idea also came from her experience growing up in China, where she noticed that children could have very limited access to educational resources and materials, depending on their families and schools. She carried that observation with her to the US and began thinking about how used books could help bridge those gaps in access. Education is something that should be a basic human right, and nobody should be left behind because of a lack of money.As Fan explained, she wanted learning to be less of a financial burden for students and their families. Textbooks, in particular, can be expensive, even when students need them for only a limited period.From used AP textbooks to more than 7,000 booksFan first approached five students at her high school with the idea of passing on the AP books they had finished using to students who could not afford them. The initiative was initially called AP Cycle, reflecting its focus on helping educational materials find new readers instead of remaining unused after exams.The project later became Literacy Cycle as its work expanded beyond textbooks. Today, the organisation accepts different kinds of reading and learning materials, including books for younger children and SAT preparation guides.In a September 2026 profile published by Points of Light, Fan described the work involved in running the initiative, from organising book drives and sorting donations to contacting community organisations, coordinating distributions and recruiting volunteers. The organisation also encourages students to establish and manage their own chapters, helping the project reach communities beyond Fan’s immediate area.The work involves more than collecting books and packing them into boxes. Fan has spoken about learning to approach organisations, build partnerships and follow up when initial emails go unanswered. She said that researching the right contacts and reaching out to people directly involved in book transportation helped her establish connections that made international distribution possible.How Literacy Cycle reaches children in the US and abroadLiteracy Cycle now works with several organisations in Maryland to distribute books to readers who can benefit from them. One of its partners, Books for International Goodwill, helps send books to countries including Gambia, Nigeria and Uganda. The nonprofit has also worked with the Children of Incarcerated Parents Partnership and the Asian American Center of Frederick.Since 2022, the organisation has distributed more than 7,000 books. The books are not limited to one age group or subject. While used AP textbooks can help students prepare for advanced classes, children’s books give younger readers the chance to discover stories and interests of their own. For Fan, a book that one student has finished using may still be useful to someone else, whether it helps them explore a new subject, prepare for an exam or find a story they enjoy.What Sophia Fan plans to do nextFan received a Daily Point of Light award from the nonprofit Points of Light in recognition of her volunteer work. The recognition, she told PEOPLE, was meaningful to her, and she hopes it will encourage other young people to take up community initiatives of their own.Despite managing Literacy Cycle alongside school and other commitments, Fan hopes to continue overseeing the organisation when she goes to college. She plans to study public or global health and explore health disparities around the world, an interest that also reflects her concern about unequal access to resources.Her advice to other students is to begin with a cause they care about rather than waiting until they have every detail figured out. In her own case, the first step was finding books that were no longer being used and looking for organisations that could put them to use.Four years later, that simple effort has developed into a network distributing thousands of books across borders. For Fan, the idea remains much the same: educational material that one person has finished with can still open up new possibilities for someone else.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Algeria’s military deployment to Niger: What’s behind the move?
articles.summary: This will be Algeria’s first foreign troop deployment in 50 years as the country shifts its military doctrine.
articles.body:
Algeria’s parliament has approved a proposal to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger, in a major shift in the North African nation’s noninterventionist military doctrine.

Algeria’s lower house, the People’s National Assembly, ratified the deployment on Sunday after the upper house, the Council of the Nation, unanimously approved the proposal earlier in the day.

Details about the number of soldiers and when they will be deployed have yet to be made public.

It comes nearly two months after Algeria dispatched four Russian-made Sukhoi Su-30 jets, a transport aircraft and an aerial refuelling aircraft to Niamey, following what Algerian authorities described as an attempt to destabilise Niger’s military-led government.

The step comes amid a thawing of relations between Algiers and Niamey as Niger’s President Abdourahamane Tchiani visited Algeria in February and, months later, his defence minister, Salifou Mody, ⁠⁠travelled to Algiers to discuss security cooperation.

The shooting down of a Malian drone by the Algerian army last April triggered a diplomatic crisis after Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso recalled their ambassadors from Algiers. The condemnation of the 2023 coup in Niger by Algeria had also strained ties.

The troop deployment is reportedly intended to protect oil installations belonging to Algeria’s state-owned energy company, Sonatrach. Troops would be sent “to protect Algeria’s economic and strategic interests, particularly its oil facilities in Niger”, The Associated Press news agency reported, quoting Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti.

It also comes as Algiers seeks to deepen security cooperation in the Sahel, a vast belt of territory stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, including several countries along Algeria’s southern frontier.

Algeria has historically been reluctant to deploy its armed forces beyond its borders, reflecting a longstanding foreign policy built around sovereignty, noninterference and opposition to foreign military intervention.

But that does not mean it has never done so.

Algerian forces participated in the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, although overseas military deployments have remained exceptionally rare in the decades since.

A constitutional revision in 2020 formalised the conditions under which Algerian troops could be sent abroad.

Under Article 91, the president may authorise such deployments, provided they receive the backing of at least two-thirds of the members of each chamber of parliament.

The constitution also provides for Algerian participation in peacekeeping operations under the auspices of the United Nations, the African Union and the Arab League.

The move is particularly significant given Algeria’s military capabilities. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the country spent more than $25bn on its armed forces in 2025, making it Africa’s largest military spender.

But the decision also comes against a backdrop of growing diplomatic tensions and shifting regional alliances.

In September, Algeria severed diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, accusing Abu Dhabi of repeated “hostile” and “provocative actions” without publicly detailing the incidents behind the decision.

The two countries have long disagreed over several regional issues, including Western Sahara and the UAE’s alleged interference in North African and Sahelian affairs.

Taken together, these developments suggest that Algeria is becoming increasingly willing to assert its security interests beyond its borders, even as it continues to emphasise the principles of sovereignty and noninterference.

For Algeria, instability in the Sahel is not a distant security concern.

The country shares thousands of kilometres of borders with Mali, Niger and Libya, making developments in its southern neighbourhood particularly consequential.

The roots of the current security crisis can be traced, in part, to the collapse of Muammar Gaddafi’s government in Libya in 2011.

At the height of the Arab Spring uprisings, Algeria took a firm stance against foreign military intervention and warned that the disintegration of the Libyan state could destabilise neighbouring countries.

Following Gaddafi’s overthrow, weapons and armed fighters, including Tuareg who had served in Libya, spread into neighbouring countries.

Their return helped fuel a rebellion in northern Mali in 2012, contributing to a security crisis that preceded the military overthrow of President Amadou Toumani Toure that March.

Over the following decade, armed rebellion expanded across parts of the Sahel, particularly Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.

Since 2012, those three countries alone have experienced six military coups: three in Mali, two in Burkina Faso and one in Niger.

Many of the coups unfolded against a backdrop of deteriorating security, with military leaders accusing civilian governments of failing to contain increasingly powerful armed groups.

But insecurity was not the only factor. Political grievances, governance failures and rivalries within armed forces also contributed to the coups.

Another factor shaping Algeria’s calculations is the changing presence of foreign military forces across the region.

For more than a decade, France was a central player in counterterrorism operations in the Sahel, deploying thousands of troops to combat armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).

But that military presence has largely unravelled.

Following successive coups and deteriorating diplomatic relations, France withdrew its troops from Mali in August 2022, Burkina Faso in February 2023 and Niger in December 2023.

The withdrawals were accompanied by growing anti-French sentiment and demands from military governments for greater control over their security policies.

Niger demanded the departure of approximately 1,500 French soldiers following its July 2023 coup.

Just months later, in April 2024, approximately 100 Russian military personnel arrived in Niamey, bringing equipment and providing training to Nigerien forces.

The personnel were associated with Africa Corps, a Russian paramilitary group close to the Kremlin.

Moscow has also expanded its military cooperation with Mali and Burkina Faso, where Russian personnel have undertaken training, advisory and security roles, including combat support in Mali.

The United States has also seen its military footprint shrink.

In 2024, Washington withdrew approximately 1,000 soldiers from Niger after the military government terminated their security cooperation agreement. The withdrawal included personnel stationed at an important US drone base near Agadez.

The result has been a significant realignment of the Sahel’s security partnerships, with Western military forces departing and Russia assuming a more prominent role.

For Algiers, the proposed deployment to Niger carries immediate security and wider strategic implications.

At the most practical level, protecting Algerian energy investments would help safeguard the country’s economic interests in a region affected by armed rebellions and political instability, including the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), which would transport Nigerian gas to Europe and traverse Niger and Algeria.

It could also deepen cooperation with Niger, whose military government has sought new security partners since taking power in 2023.

More broadly, the move would allow Algeria to establish a direct military presence in a neighbouring country at a time when the Sahel’s security architecture is being reshaped.

“We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure,” Senator Boulghiti told reporters after the vote. “It is simply an adaptation of our doctrine to evolving circumstances so we can rise to the new challenges imposed by the situation in the Sahel region.”

articles.title: Election season hits overdrive for thousands of Israeli Americans
articles.summary: Dual citizens of the U.S. and Israel are staring down two consequential elections in the coming days, with thousands preparing to hop on planes to have their voices heard in both countries. While the U.S. allows absentee voting, Israel requires voting in person. And an estimated 67,000 Israelis worldwide are expected to travel back to…
articles.body:
Dual citizens of the U.S. and Israel are staring down two consequential elections in the coming days, with thousands preparing to hop on planes to have their voices heard in both countries.

While the U.S. allows absentee voting, Israel requires voting in person. And an estimated 67,000 Israelis worldwide are expected to travel back to the country to vote in the Oct. 27 contest.

The vote in Israel is largely viewed as a referendum on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, between those who view him as responsible for the atrocities of Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attacks and the country’s global isolation, and those who believe Netanyahu is the only leader strong enough to defeat Israel’s many enemies.

Israeli expats represent a small percentage of the more than seven million Israelis eligible to vote. But election experts say that about 40,000 votes translate into at least one seat in Israel’s Parliament, the Knesset. For the dozens of competing parties, one seat can mean crucial leverage in coalition negotiations.

“I don’t usually vote in a country I don’t live in, it’s not my day-to-day life and I won’t feel the effects of that vote in the same way that my family who live there will,” said Solomon, 30, a dual U.S.-Israeli citizen and self-described progressive. He asked to be identified only by his first name to protect his privacy.

“This election is so consequential that I believe I have a duty to act and to have my voice heard — especially when so many voices impacted by this government may not be.”

He is flying from his home in Washington, D.C., to Israel to vote, and then coming back to the U.S. to canvass in Michigan.

In Israel, he’s trying to use his vote to unseat Netanyahu, concerned over the prime minister’s ultranationalist and religious policies, and actions toward Arab citizens and Palestinians. He’s also weighing how those policies contribute to Israel’s global isolation and put a target on Jewish communities abroad.

“I’m trying to figure out if a shift in the Israeli election can kind of shift the narrative in the U.S.,” he said.

Israel is a lightning rod in American politics, and the future of U.S.-Israel relations has risen in priority for the Nov. 3 elections. Voters are increasingly concerned about how the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran is leading to greater insecurity at home, while American views of the Israeli government and Israeli people have grown increasingly negative across the political spectrum.

In Michigan, Solomon will be canvassing for a pro-Israel, Jewish Democrat. And while he’s attracted to Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s progressive bona fides, Solomon is concerned about anti-Israel sentiment in the Democratic Party pushing the boundaries of antisemitism, particularly on the far left.

“There’s some things I don’t love, and I’m moderately concerned about. But at the same time, this is a progressive wave that I want to see,” he said.

Solomon is traveling with his mother, also Israeli, back to Israel to vote, paying about $1,600 each for flights from the U.S. to Portugal, and then a charter flight to Israel.

The charter flight was arranged by AID Coalition, a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization that is helping Israelis abroad travel back to vote. Jonathan Barsade, president of AID Coalition, said the group organized a charter flight from Lisbon after flight cancellations left Israelis trying to transit through the country without a flight to Israel.

It’s part of the organization’s “Fly & Vote” campaign to encourage Israelis abroad to vote. The group doesn’t provide direct financial assistance or incentives to vote — to avoid potential legal issues — but helps voters get to Israel and make sure they are registered to cast a ballot.

Barsade, a dual U.S.-Israeli citizen who is planning to vote in both countries, said Israelis abroad could account for about 10 percent of voter participation and called the law requiring in-person voting “anachronistic.”

Barsade said that today’s interconnected world makes Israelis living abroad more connected to the daily issues in Israel.

“They might be residing abroad physically, but emotionally, mentally, they’re in both countries,” he said.

Only a narrow set of people are allowed to vote from abroad, including diplomats and Israelis who work for the Jewish Agency, an Israeli national institution. And while there’s no real political movement pushing for wider access to absentee voting, there is debate over whether more Israelis should be allowed to vote from abroad if only traveling temporarily during elections.

For Mor Erez, 37, the burden of traveling to Israel is robbing her husband and friends of their chance to vote, when a few thousand votes can make a difference. In 2022, the historic left-wing party Meretz was about 4,000 votes short of the electoral threshold, left out of the Knesset for the first time since 1992.

“My husband told me that he really wants to come vote with me, but he knows that he will wake up the day after not voting and will live with himself, but he knows that I will not,” she said. “This is the mutual decision we made because we can’t afford for both of us to go and the kids.”

Erez is spending approximately $2,000 to fly back to Israel from her home in North Carolina. She’s been in the U.S. for about 14 months, describing a difficult decision to leave Israel amid financial, physical and emotional hardship from Hamas’s attack and Israel’s subsequent, multi-front wars.

“Although we are here, it doesn’t mean that Israel is not ours. It’s still our home. We still fight for it, and we still suffer from things that happen there, here,” she said. Erez described the feeling of judgment from people when she reveals she’s Israeli, and that she has to answer for the Israeli government and all the associated criticisms.

Erez said she doesn’t view her vote as “anti-Netanyahu,” but is voting to change the leadership who were in place and failed to prevent Hamas’s attack. She’s also traumatized from the heavy burden on her family from her husband’s long military service, and the fraught debate in the country over the ultra-Orthodox community’s reliance on state services without having to serve in the military or national service.

David, 49, a dual U.S.-Israeli citizen living in Jerusalem, will vote in Israel and then travel to the U.S. to vote in Maine’s election, where long-time Republican Sen. Susan Collins is facing a tight race against the Democratic nominee, Troy Jackson, and could influence which party controls the Senate. David is using a pseudonym to protect his privacy.

He doesn’t center his Maine vote on which candidate is good for Israel, but he sees parallels in both elections with the debate around term limits. Collins has been a senator for nearly 30 years. Likewise, Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having served a total of 20 years since 1996.

“Someone can’t just stay in power forever just because they’ve been in power a long time. So in some ways, it’s a little bit like Israel,” he said.

For his vote in Israel, David is concerned about the future of the country, the wars with no end in sight, the increasing global isolation and the increased divide in America over ties with Israel.

David saw President Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu as confirming Israel’s seclusion.

“That really is a disturbing feeling, that Israel basically has only one potential tie with the United States, and that’s the president,” he said.

“The problem is that the other candidates that are running don’t seem to present a strong vision either, and that is a huge problem.”

articles.title: Man says Texas Roadhouse served him $20 steak instead of pricier filet multiple times
articles.summary: Kenneth Card claims a Texas Roadhouse in Forsyth, Illinois, served him sirloin instead of filet mignon three times, sparking a viral TikTok debate.
articles.body: A loyal Texas Roadhouse customer is going viral after claiming he repeatedly got a cheaper cut of steak than what he ordered, leaving him wondering if he was being ripped off. Kenneth Card took to TikTok in early October to warn other customers that he received a sirloin instead of a filet mignon three times at a Texas Roadhouse in Forsyth, Illinois. His post has since gotten over 30,000 views. Card told Fox News Digital that his experience working in hotel and restaurant kitchens preparing and cutting steaks made him confident he could tell the difference. MEAT EXPERT SHARES THE MISTAKE MOST AMERICANS MAKE WHEN COOKING STEAK "I know what types of meat I get whenever I receive it," Card said. Card said he has been going to the Texas Roadhouse location about once a week for over a year, and had even built a rapport with staff. The first time it happened, he told staff he thought he had received the wrong steak and they gave him a filet. On his next visit, he said, he ate the steak without raising the issue. When he ordered filet mignon again on a third visit, Card said, he spoke with a manager. EXPERTS REVEAL HOW TO SPOT FAKE 'WAGYU' SO YOU DON’T GET RIPPED OFF ON PREMIUM BEEF "I was like, 'Look, this is the third time that y'all tried to sell me a sirloin or whatever else kind of steak it is besides a filet,'" he recalled. The restaurant took the steak away to get a second opinion, Card said, and staff told him it was not what he had ordered. He said he waited for a new one, asked for it to go and posted his video after getting home. "I just wanted to get the word out that, 'Hey, you're getting ripped off if you're ordering this, and they're selling you this,'" Card said. He said he was surprised by the attention and just wanted to make sure people are getting what they pay for. A spokesperson for the company said it has "not been able to track that this occurred on three occasions," but confirmed it was corrected onsite once. Management "quickly made it right," the spokesperson said. Some commenters said it was likely just an issue with that specific location, while others admitted they wouldn't know the difference between the two cuts. "For those of us who don't know the difference, they would get by with that," one man said. "Fortunately, you happen to know the difference." articles.title: Key European defence ministers meet in Paris to discuss Ukraine support
articles.summary: Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK to discuss increasing military assistance to Ukraine.
articles.body:
Defence ministers of key European countries are meeting in the French capital to discuss military support for Ukraine amid continuing Russia-Ukraine attacks.

A Russian strike on ⁠Ukraine’s southeastern city ⁠of Zaporizhzhia injured four people on Monday morning, according to regional Governor Mykhailo Semikin, while a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Voronezh killed two people and wounded 17, regional Governor Alexander Gusev said.

In Ukraine, two more people were injured in Russian strikes on the Chernihiv region, Ukraine’s emergency service ⁠said on Telegram on Monday.

The Russian Ministry of Defence also claimed its forces hit a power station in ‌Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, as well as a nearby warehouse, and a power station in the Khmelnytskyi region.

The ministry said Russian forces also targeted port infrastructure in Chornomorsk in southwestern Ukraine, and a cargo vessel en route to Odesa, which it claimed was being used for military purposes.

Meanwhile, officials say that many of those wounded in the Ukrainian drone attack on Voronezh were passengers on a commuter train hit by falling debris.

“A significant number of the injured, including two seriously wounded, were on a train that was moving in the left-bank suburb of Voronezh when debris from a UAV fell on it,” Gusev said on Telegram.

The attack also caused fires at “a number of industrial businesses (without significant damage), a business centre in the central part of the city, and a residential building”, the governor added.

Four and a half years into the war, attacks have been escalating between Ukrainian and Russian forces, with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries and Russian forces bombarding Ukraine with relentless air strikes.

Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi, UAE, in the first half of November.

Meanwhile, defence ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom are set to meet in Paris on Monday to discuss additional support for Ukraine, European defence and the regional conflict in the Middle East, according to French officials.

At their previous meeting in Berlin in June, the five major European powers pledged continued support for Ukraine, seeking to send a clear signal to Moscow that Europe remains firmly behind Kyiv.

In an interview aired ⁠on Sunday, Zelenskyy said for Kyiv to halt the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which US President Donald Trump has demanded, Moscow must stop hitting Ukraine’s power ‌infrastructure.

Zelenskyy said if the Russians continue to hit Ukraine’s power infrastructure, the US should be willing to allow the use of Starshield over Russia to detect missile ‌launch ‌sites, or supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles.

Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version, Starshield, were now fully functional after ⁠more than a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.

articles.title: Trump critic Lula wins reelection in Brazil
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a critic of President Trump and a champion of the Latin American left, won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday in a runoff election against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil’s former far-right leader Jair Bolsonaro. “We made history in the streets and at the ballot boxes, with…
articles.body:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a critic of President Trump and a champion of the Latin American left, won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday in a runoff election against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil’s former far-right leader Jair Bolsonaro.

“We made history in the streets and at the ballot boxes, with the people as the protagonists of a journey that still has a long way to go,” the president, commonly known as Lula, wrote on the social platform X. “Democracy prevailed, hope grew stronger, and Brazil moves forward. This victory is ours. And we’re going to do so much more together!”

Brazil’s electoral court announced that Lula led by nearly 4.4 million votes over Flávio Bolsonaro, with 51.8 percent of ballots cast.

Lula, who began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader and the founder of the Workers’ Party, campaigned on the cost of living and security in a country that has faced years of internal violence. He previously served as president from 2003 to 2011, before handing the presidency to Cabinet minister Dilma Rousseff, who was impeached in 2016.

The announcement of Lula’s victory came after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered polls to remain open for two additional hours, at the request of both candidates, with Lula citing transportation issues for voters and Bolsonaro pointing to flooding in his southern strongholds.

Bolsonaro quickly rejected the election’s outcome and called for the results to be annulled. He claimed that Zanin, a former lawyer of Lula’s, had changed “the rules of the game in the middle of the game.”

“I do not recognize this,” Bolsonaro told supporters, according to Al Jazeera . “There is no way I can accept this outrage that was committed against Brazil. I will take legal action and I will not give up on Brazil.”

Trump, who supported Bolsonaro’s campaign, has not commented on Lula’s win. But his son, Donald Trump Jr., criticized the outcome.

“If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause,” he wrote on the social platform X .

The State Department had previously sought to help restore the Bolsonaros to power in the lead-up to the election, Reuters reported .

Trump has often been compared to Bolsonaro’s father, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after he lost the 2022 presidential election to Lula.

World leaders heaped praise on Lula for his victory. One of Latin America’s few remaining left-wing leaders, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, congratulated Lula on his win.

“Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” she wrote on X .

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, in congratulating Lula, wrote on X that the relationship between their countries “has flourished under our partnership.”

“Let’s seize this opportunity to make it even stronger, together — to create major new trade opportunities, protect the environment, and build greater prosperity for both our peoples,” he added.

articles.title: Murderer’s bid to eat Vegemite in Australian prison rejected by judge
articles.summary: A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state’s ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.”
articles.body: A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state’s ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.” Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year. He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to “enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background,” court documents showed. Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities’ refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite “limited his cultural rights” under the charter. But she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities’ goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system. “The limitation on Mr. McKechnie’s ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner,” Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment. Alcohol brewing and sniffer dogs Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state’s 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs’ ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content. McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were “less restrictive means reasonably available” to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes. Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80% of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who weren’t raised on it. The last US president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: “It’s horrible.” Vitamin deficiency claims McKechnie had initially testified that the lack of Vegemite had contributed to his thiamine deficiency. He said both Vegemite and pork were sources of thiamine, also known as vitamin B1. As a Jew who observed kosher law, he told the court he couldn’t eat pork either and took daily doses of the vitamin. Vegemite has long been marketed as a source of B vitamins thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3) and folate (B9) which are promoted as healthy additions to the diets of growing children. But McKechnie dropped the thiamine issue as “not important,” after lawyers for the prison authorities objected to his evidence. ‘Deprived, sad and disconnected’ McKechnie said not eating Vegemite made him feel “deprived of being able to practice my Australian culture, sad and disconnected from my family and community.” The judge responded that “it is difficult to accept that the inability to consume Vegemite, rather than the fact of his imprisonment, is a material cause of his sadness and disconnection from his family and community.” McKechnie cited an article published in the food studies journal “Gastronomica” in 2003 that said, “Vegemite may be the best predictor of national identity of any food in the world.” The article, based on research by Australia’s Queensland University in 1995, found that a “taste for the spread strongly correlates with early exposure and to Australian birth and ancestry.” McKechnie also referred to the Australian Olympic Committee overturning an Chinese import ban on Vegemite ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing. He cited Australian band Men at Work’s 1980s international hit “Down Under” that mentions a “Vegemite sandwich.” On the effectiveness of smearing contraband with Vegemite, McKechnie cited a Melbourne newspaper article from 2017 that reported a man’s unsuccessful attempt to use the odor of the spread to conceal illicit drugs that he attempted to smuggle into a music festival in Victoria. The attempt was thwarted by police sniffer dogs. Judge rejects claims The judge upheld prison authorities’ argument that McKechnie had failed to provide any proper foundations for his opinion that Vegemite does not interfere with drug sniffer dogs. McKechnie also argued that Vegemite contained “no live yeast” and that any piece of fruit would be more useful in making alcohol than the spread. A state prison department manager, Kevin White, cited publicly available research that said Vegemite helped home-brewed beer ferment more quickly. Vegemite’s owner, Bega Group, did not respond to a request for comment on Monday.

articles.title: Police arrest a 15-year-old in shooting near Florida A&M stadium that injured 12
articles.summary: A 15-year-old male has been arrested in connection with a shooting close to Florida A&M University’s Bragg Memorial Stadium over the weekend that injured 12 people, according to police.
articles.body: A 15-year-old male has been arrested in connection with a shooting close to Florida A&M University’s Bragg Memorial Stadium over the weekend that injured 12 people, according to police. The Tallahassee Police Department said Monday that detectives had arrested the teenager Sunday in connection with the shooting. The teenager is facing 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent. “What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families,” Police Chief Lawrence Revell said. “While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy,” he added. The shooting broke out about 8 p.m. Saturday, near Perry and Manatee streets, close to the stadium, where homecoming celebrations included a football game. The 12 people injured included minors. One individual also sustained an ankle injury while fleeing the gunfire, police said. After the shooting took place, the university issued a statement on X asking members of its campus community to stay away from the area. It described the shooting as having taken place “near campus,” which it said remained safe. “Our hearts are with the victims and everyone affected by tonight’s incident on Perry Street,” the university added. Police said Monday that they were continuing to investigate the incident but that preliminary findings indicated “a physical altercation occurred before shots were fired” and that “the incident stemmed from a dispute between individuals known to one another.” They added that “none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets.” Additional arrests are possible, Tallahassee police said, as the investigation continues.

articles.title: Couple campaigns to save their wedding venue hotel in Weymouth
articles.summary: The Riviera Hotel in Weymouth has been closed since 2022.
articles.body:
A couple are campaigning to save the hotel where they got married after the building has been derelict for four years.

Tess and Des Shephard celebrated their wedding at the Riviera Hotel in Weymouth in 2018 before the building went on to close in 2022 following storm damage.

Tess, who is behind the Revive the Riviera campaign to get new ownership at the hotel said it was "a lovely building" and she was just seeing what she could do to help.

The grade II listed building, which was built in 1936 was purchased by Saudi based owners in 2009 under the company Bowleaze Limited.

The Shephards currently live in Surrey but Tess said they have hopes to move down to Weymouth in the future.

She called the current state of the hotel "very sad" and believed that it could be "a gold mine" for the local community "if looked after properly".

She said they have about 60 people in support of their campaign to find new ownership for the site.

Tess said: "The Riviera has come to mean a lot. It's such an iconic building.

"It would be a shame to knock it down and turn it into luxury flats that no one can afford."

More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

This includes requiring the owner to make the property safe or the council taking emergency action to make the building safe.

South Dorset MP Lloyd Hatton said people are "frustrated" to see the building fall into disrepair.

He said local people are "paying the price for a building that is unloved, unused and allowed basically to fall into the sea".

Hatton said his priority is getting the hotel bought back from overseas ownership and he stated that they have had interest from local businesses.

The BBC has been unable to contact the current owner of the Riviera Hotel for a comment.

articles.title: 'Rising runoff, flood risks': Fresh warning over China’s mega Brahmaputra dam
articles.summary: Chinese researchers have warned that the Brahmaputra River could witness increased runoff and a higher risk of floods over the course of this century,
articles.body: Chinese researchers have warned that the Brahmaputra River could witness increased runoff and a higher risk of floods over the course of this century, raising fresh concerns over the potential implications of Beijing’s $168-billion mega dam project on the river in Tibet.Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Yunnan University reconstructed the river’s runoff history from 1325 to 2020 using tree-ring width data collected from the southeastern Tibetan Plateau. Combining the reconstruction with climate data, they developed a model projecting an increase in river runoff under future climate scenarios, alongside a possible rise in high-runoff events such as floods.The findings were published in the journal China Science Bulletin on October 8, the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post reported on Monday, according to PTI.The river, known as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, flows into India as the Siang in Arunachal Pradesh before becoming the Brahmaputra further downstream. It is a crucial source of water for agriculture, livelihoods and ecosystems across northeastern India and Bangladesh.“These results provide a long-term perspective on hydroclimatic variability in the Yarlung Tsangpo River and a scientific basis for assessing future water-resource risks,” the researchers said.They called for projected changes in runoff to be considered while planning water-resource development and storage infrastructure, as well as when assessing risks involving rivers that cross international borders.What is runoff?Runoff is a natural process in the water cycle in which excess water flows over the land or through the soil into rivers, streams, lakes and other bodies of water. It occurs when rainfall, melting snow or irrigation water exceeds the amount that the ground can absorb. Although runoff helps replenish water sources, excessive runoff can cause environmental and property damage.Runoff can carry pollutants, including fertilisers, pesticides, oil and other chemicals, into surface water and groundwater, harming wildlife and potentially affecting human health. Excessive runoff can also cause flooding, soil erosion and property damage, particularly in urban areas with impermeable surfaces. Measures such as effective drainage systems, vegetation cover and mulch can help reduce runoff and minimise its harmful effects.What we know about the projectEstimated to cost around $168 billion, the project is expected to comprise five cascade hydropower stations.While the project is primarily intended to generate electricity, its scale and upstream location have raised questions about downstream water flows, flood management and ecological impacts. A large upstream project could give China some ability to regulate the timing and volume of releases, although the extent of any impact on India would depend on its design and operation.The latest findings add to scientific concerns about the risks associated with the project. In July, Chinese geologists warned that an active fault line beneath the planned dam could threaten its structural stability. They urged engineers to strengthen vulnerable slopes and introduce protective measures against landslides and rock collapses.The Himalayan region’s vulnerability to cascading natural hazards was also highlighted by flash floods along the China-Nepal border on August 26, triggered by an ice-and-rock avalanche and the subsequent collapse of a temporary river blockage. articles.title: How did Lula beat Bolsonaro after losing Brazil’s first-round election?
articles.summary: Brazil’s president secured a historic fourth term after overturning a first-round defeat.
articles.body:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has achieved a stunning election victory, defeating far-right rival Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, despite trailing him by more than two million votes in the first round held earlier in October.

The 80-year-old leftist secured an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, becoming the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985 to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round.

“I just had to tell you that I love you. Tomorrow, the fight continues,” Lula told cheering fans at a victory parade in Sao Paulo. “No one is required to like the president-elect, but he must govern for everyone.”

Lula’s victory is a significant setback for the right-wing political movement that has gained ground across Latin America, often with the backing of United States President Donald Trump.

So how did Lula turn things around in just three weeks, and what challenges does he face?

Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, secured 51.79 percent of valid votes , or 64.26 million ballots, compared with Bolsonaro’s 48.21 percent, or 59.83 million votes, according to the final tally.

The result marked a dramatic reversal from the October 4 first round, when Bolsonaro won 47.03 percent against Lula’s 45.16 percent, a lead of approximately 2.2 million votes.

Turnout on Sunday was 80.8 percent, nearly 2 percent higher than the previous round, when 78.92 percent of the electorate cast their votes.

Bolsonaro refused to concede and called for the run-off result to be annulled after Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered voting to be extended by two hours. Both candidates had requested extensions, citing transport disruptions and severe weather.

The controversy echoes the aftermath of the 2022 election, when Flavio’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept his defeat. He was subsequently convicted of plotting a coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison, which he is serving under house arrest.

However, experts say Flavio faces significant obstacles in overturning the result.

Vinicius G. Rodrigues Vieira, an economics and international relations professor at the Armando Alvares Penteado Foundation, told Al Jazeera that Bolsonaro’s legal arguments were weak, particularly because his own campaign had requested an extension.

“I don’t think that will resonate in the courts, but certainly will help Bolsonarismo, the far-right movement here in Brazil, to remain politically strong on the streets,” he said.

Lula’s comeback was driven by a revitalised grassroots campaign, youth mobilisation and a shift towards digital campaigning, analysts said.

Al Jazeera correspondent Monica Yanakiew, reporting from Sao Paulo, said young Brazilians spontaneously organised online after Bolsonaro’s first-round victory, creating what became known as “Lula’s army”.

“It was this army that went to the streets, millions of people across Brazil, and young people just mobilised themselves, energised the campaign, which frankly was not very energised at all before the first round,” she said.

Editor-in-chief of The Brazilian Report, Gustavo Ribeiro, told Al Jazeera that Lula’s campaign had initially appeared complacent.

“Lula’s campaign also got its act together after a first round in which it acted as if this election was in the bag and essentially running an anachronistic, mostly offline campaign,” he said.

“The campaign really pivoted towards a digital mentality and a grassroots effort,” Ribeiro said, adding that Lula had used “the power of incumbency very cleverly in his favour”.

“I would say this is more the merit of Lula, even if Bolsonaro just worked to run off the clock.”

Other experts agreed, saying Bolsonaro’s own mistakes were likely to have contributed to his defeat. Academic Vieira argued that the senator had become overconfident after winning the first round.

“In the first week, he was already behaving as if he were already the president-elect. He was appointing ministers,” the economics professor pointed out.

“If there is something Brazilian people don’t like [it’s] arrogance, so Mr. Flavio is paying a very high price for this,” he added.

The Brazilian Report’s Ribeiro also questioned Bolsonaro’s political appeal.

“He does not have his father’s charisma. He was essentially running on his father’s last name,” he said.

Higher turnout was another important factor.

An estimated 33.4 million Brazilians abstained in the first round, representing about 21 percent of the electorate. Abstention fell to approximately 19 percent in the run-off.

Fernando Brancoli, an international relations professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said previously absent voters appeared to have participated in the second round.

“We already know that a large number of people who didn’t vote [in] the first round, they now showed up,” he told Al Jazeera.

Brancoli also suggested some first-round Bolsonaro voters may have switched to Lula, although detailed voting patterns remain unclear.

According to Vieira, the election was arguably one of the most consequential in Brazil’s history.

After the 21-year dictatorship ended in 1985, he said Brazil built a “constitutional setting” which provided social rights to the population more than at any time in the South American nation’s history.

“That’s so important for the Brazilian people because we still have high levels of inequality,” he said, noting that it was crucial to “keep a very high degree of political participation”.

In contrast, the far-right Bolsonarismo movement had tried to “curtail voting rights” by employing “voting suppression tactics”, Vieira said.

Despite his victory, Lula faces a conservative-dominated Congress that could severely restrict his legislative agenda.

Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies could control more than 280 seats out of 513 in the lower house, and up to 50 out of a total of 81 Senate seats, potentially giving the opposition majorities in both chambers.

Brancoli warned that Lula would have limited room to manoeuvre.

“We can definitely expect Lula’s government [is] not going to be able to push for a broad agenda. You’ll get small wins, and you’ll have to negotiate with those groups,” he said.

Economic pressures pose another considerable challenge. Brazil’s public debt has exceeded 82 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), according to the World Bank, while the government forecasts growth of just 2.3 percent next year.

Moreover, Brancoli asserted that Lula would also need to address security and household debt, two issues that helped make the election competitive.

The president’s age raises further questions about the future of his Workers’ Party (PT), and who would replace the longtime leader, Brancoli noted.

“There’s no one that could substitute him, and he’s older,” he said.

articles.title: Israel expands expulsions in occupied West Bank to cement control
articles.summary: Israel escalates forced expulsions and infrastructure destruction with the goal of imposing ‘new reality’, analysts say.
articles.body:
More than 3,000 Palestinians have been forced from their homes in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron as the Israeli army escalates a sweeping military operation that human rights experts describe as a calculated effort to permanently displace the Palestinian population.

Israel has imposed a lockdown across the city and detained at least 71 people over the past four days, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.

Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin said on Monday a total of 488 families comprising 3,171 people had been displaced across the wider governorate, while Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told Al Jazeera that 3,043 of those forced from their homes are from within Hebron city limits alone.

Separately, the Israeli military continues a demolition campaign that has resulted in the destruction of residential buildings, factories and roads, while also blocking roads, raiding homes and assaulting Palestinians.

The crackdown has been in place since Friday, when two soldiers were killed in a shooting near the city. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has justified it by pledging an operation “unseen” since the 1967 war.

It comes amid increased tensions across the occupied West Bank as Israeli settlers and soldiers engage in violent pogroms. Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife as aggression has been on the rise before Israel’s general election on Tuesday, in which Netanyahu is seeking re-election.

According to municipal authorities in Hebron, the majority of the forcibly displaced Palestinians are women, children and elderly individuals.

Israeli soldiers, meanwhile, have systematically converted dozens of homes of the uprooted Palestinian families into military barracks and field interrogation centres.

“The measures taken in the city of Hebron are not of a single type, but rather have surpassed any idea of temporary evacuation or deportation,” said Noman Amr, a professor of contemporary history at al-Quds Open University, Dura branch in Hebron, as he explained the multifaceted nature of the displacement. “Evacuating homes falls into three categories: evacuation for demolition, evacuation for revenge and collective punishment, and evacuation for military uses, where they have turned some homes into military barracks.”

Amr also highlighted the psychological warfare at play. “This aggressive, collective punitive, terrorist, racist behaviour aims to create a state of panic, fear and instability for the Palestinian society,” he said, quoting displaced residents who said they heard soldiers make comments such as, “You will return to your homes on Judgement Day”.

The ultimate goal, Amr added, is “to impose a new reality” that can be summarised “in one sentence: ‘more land, fewer Arabs'”.

Israeli officials explicitly linked the Hebron operation to previous campaigns in the occupied West Bank. Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced their intention to apply the “Jenin camp model” to Hebron, which involves forced evacuation of residents, inspecting homes, confiscating weapons and bulldozing roads.

Rights groups have compared the current attack on Hebron with the tactics used during the “Iron Wall” operation in early 2025 in the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps, which killed at least 102 people, displaced more than 33,000 and destroyed over half of their residential buildings.

Katz previously said the aggressive tactics in Jenin represented “the first lesson from the method of repeated raids in Gaza”, where Israel’s genocidal three-year war has killed more than 74,000 people and left the vast majority of the territory in ruins.

The resulting destruction left the Jenin camp “nearly uninhabitable”, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

Last month, a UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR) report warned that the Israeli military’s actions at the three camps “appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing”. Displaced Palestinians reported being told by Israeli officers that there would be no more refugee camps and that they should “all go to Jordan”.

Israeli forces killed at least 21 children during the operation, including a 10-year-old boy who was shot while waiting for his father and a two-year-old girl killed while having dinner with her family.

Analysts also pointed to the systematic destruction of vital infrastructure during the Hebron operation with the goal of making displacement permanent.

“Targeting the main infrastructure by the occupation army forces is a targeting of the life and stability of the Palestinian human being,” said Amr. He specified that targeting water wells “exceeds their direct material value, but rather relates to existence, stability and continuity”.

Amr also outlined the deep collaboration between the Israeli army and armed settler groups. “Settlers today in Hebron and other places have a militia consisting of more than 150,000 people heavily armed with modern automatic weapons and four-wheel drive vehicles, and they sometimes wear the occupation army uniform,” he said.

“The army closes the place, empties homes, demolishes them, and closes roads … while settlers continue their repeated attacks on the residents, released prisoners, and commercial interests.”

This ground-level violence is paired with administrative land grabs. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC) said on Sunday the Israeli military had established 220 barriers across Hebron, severing Palestinian communities from their lands while maintaining connectivity for illegal settlements. The CRRC noted this is part of a broader network of new outposts designed to expand control over the spaces separating settlements and to besiege Palestinian expansions.

Also on Sunday, the Israeli army said in a statement that it would bar Palestinian workers from entering most areas of the West Bank through Monday and enforce a full closure of crossings into and out of the territory on Tuesday, the day of Israel’s parliamentary election.

Mayor al-Jabari accused Netanyahu and his hard-right government of exploiting the military operation to secure settler votes.

Amr echoed this sentiment. “The Palestinian pays this price as electoral propaganda for the right wing,” he said.

“They do not want Palestinians to remain in their places, but rather they propose a more advanced step, which is that they want to correct the history that allowed Palestinians to stay after the 1967 setback or even after the 1948 Nakba,” he added, using the Arabic word for “catastrophe” to refer to the ethnic cleansing of Palestine nearly 80 years ago.

articles.title: Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
articles.summary: The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.
articles.body:
Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973.

The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister, as the country seeks support against armed groups, some of which are linked to al-Qaeda or Islamic State.

Algeria has economic interests in Niger, including a planned gas pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.

The deployment comes as the two neighbours rebuild ties after a diplomatic rift in 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers.

Algeria's upper house of parliament held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on the proposed deployment. According to AFP news agency, 148 of the 174 senators voted in favour. It was later backed by the lower house of parliament.

However, the timing and number of soldiers to be deployed have not been announced.

The move would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision allowing overseas military deployments and a significant shift in Algeria's long-standing policy against sending forces abroad.

"We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after the vote.

Algeria's state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has also signed an agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry to explore for oil in the Kafra region. Two exploration wells are estimated to contain 168 million and 100 million barrels, respectively, Reuters reported.

Relations between Algeria and Niger have not always been smooth in recent years.

Algeria condemned the 2023 coup that ousted Niger's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum, and brought Gen Abdourahamane Tchiani to power.

Tensions rose again in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in solidarity with Mali, a close ally which is also under military rule.

Relations have since improved. Tchiani visited Algeria in February 2026, and in late August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to Niger to help suppress a coup attempt and also donated four military helicopters.

articles.title: Iran hosts Saudi Arabia and regional powers as fears grow of return to war
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia and its allies dispatched top security officials to Iran for talks on Monday amid fears of a fresh US-Israeli offensive that could plunge the Middle East into further instability.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia and its allies dispatched top security officials to Iran for talks on Monday amid fears of a fresh US-Israeli offensive that could plunge the Middle East into further instability. Pakistani military chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Saudi Prince Khalid bin Salman in Tehran for meetings with Iran’s top officials, including national security chief Mohsen Rezaei and President Masoud Pezeshkian. The meeting in Tehran comes at a tense moment in the Middle East as speculation grows that President Donald Trump could order new strikes on Iran after next week’s midterm elections. It also marks the first high-level contact between Iran and Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis escalated attacks against Saudi targets last month. The meeting will discuss “de-escalation” between parties involved in the “ongoing crisis,” a Saudi Foreign Ministry official, Rayed Krimly, said. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, told reporters the talks may serve as a prelude to “establishing a regional security framework.” “We have consistently emphasized that regional security can only be ensured by relying on the will and security considerations of the countries of the region,” Baghaei added. Saudi, Turkey and Pakistan represent the Mecca Alliance – a newly formed coalition of three of the region’s largest powers. The pact, under which an attack on one is deemed an attack against all, has drawn scrutiny for uniting nuclear-armed Pakistan, Turkey’s military strength and Saudi Arabia’s financial resources. Pakistan has been a key intermediary between Washington and Tehran since the war started in February. “The significance of the meeting lies primarily in its timing and the officials involved,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN. “It comes at a moment when the risk of another round of war between Iran and the United States is growing, and the three members of the Mecca Pact have direct security interests at stake.” The visit by Khalid bin Salman – a Saudi royal and brother of the kingdom’s de-facto leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman – surprised observers. Iran and Saudi Arabia represent competing religious ideologies and have been locked in a regional rivalry for decades, culminating in an outright confrontation earlier this year after the US and Israel launched a war on the Islamic Republic. Iran struck Washington’s regional allies, including Saudi Arabia, after the US and Israel killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei along with much of his military brass and top nuclear scientists in February. Iran’s allies and proxies, including those in Iraq and Yemen, have also struck Saudi oil facilities and civilian infrastructure, putting unprecedented pressure on the kingdom. Countries in the Middle East are concerned that a fresh US offensive against Iran would invite further Iranian retaliation after eight months of instability in the Middle East. Sufficient US forces are now deployed in the region to carry out the potential attacks, two US officials told CNN. The scope of new US military operations would likely go beyond efforts to simply “mow the lawn” or maintain the status quo by striking radars, launchers and other Iranian assets that can be quickly reconstituted — as has been the case since Trump halted full combat operations earlier this year, the sources added. After months of retaliatory Iranian missile and drone projectiles on its US-allied neighbors, Tehran has decreased the intensity of strikes, instead focusing its strategy on creating economic uncertainty by trying to block the only waterway used by vessels transporting a fifth of the world’s oil and gas daily. Tehran has called on countries in the region to remove US bases and end their reliance on Washington for defense. Most of Iran’s regional neighbors field militaries armed by the US, but have slowly begun diversifying their arsenals and formalizing new military alliances amid concerns over Washington’s commitment to defending its allies. The Mecca Alliance is part of a “broader effort” to develop a more “independent regional security architecture,” Danny Citrinowicz, former head of the Iran branch of Israel’s military intelligence, wrote on X. “The decision to engage directly with Tehran is equally significant,” Citrinowicz added. “It reflects not only recognition of the Iranian regime but also an understanding that Iran remains a central regional player whose influence cannot simply be ignored.” Iranian officials have welcomed the initiative, and some, including former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, see it as an opportunity to move toward a broader security framework between the region and away from dependence on the US. Yet, these developments do not yet signal an immediate diplomatic breakthrough, Azizi of the Crisis Group said. “Tehran wants credible guarantees that any agreement would prevent another military attack, and it is difficult to see how Saudi Arabia, Turkey or Pakistan could provide such guarantees or exert sufficient influence over Trump to secure them,” he said. “Unless these countries bring something new to the table that could change the calculations in either Tehran or Washington, the meeting is unlikely to produce a substantive breakthrough,” Azizi added. “For now, it looks more like a last-minute attempt to prevent the resumption of war than the beginning of a new diplomatic process.”
