articles.title: UN panel: Russia is committing crimes against humanity by targeting civilians in Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia is committing war crimes and crimes against humanity by intentionally attacking civilian infrastructure – including vital energy systems – in Ukraine, an independent UN investigations panel said on Monday.
articles.body: Russia is committing war crimes and crimes against humanity by intentionally attacking civilian infrastructure – including vital energy systems – in Ukraine, an independent UN investigations panel said on Monday. Russian forces have been targeting Ukrainian power infrastructure since the early months of the war in 2022, and massively ramped up these attacks at the beginning of last year’s winter, leaving millions of Ukrainians freezing in the darkness of their homes. A new report published by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine on Monday and shared with CNN, said these attacks “were carried out with intent” and were in line with Russia’s “state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering.” “Russian commanders who were ordering these attacks knew that the heating facilities they targeted were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter,” the report, which is being submitted to the UN General Assembly, said. CNN has approached the Kremlin for comment. Large-scale Russian drone and missile attacks last winter reduced Ukraine’s thermal power generation capacities by 70 per cent in the most affected areas, according to Kyiv. The suffering was made worse by an unusually cold winter with temperatures dropping to as low as -30 degrees Celsius (-22 F) on multiple occasions. The commission was established by the UN’s Human Rights Council just days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It has previously reported on other aspects of Russia’s war on Ukraine, including allegations of sexual and gender-based violence committed by Russian armed forces, and the wide-spread forced deportations of Ukrainian children by Russian authorities. In this latest report, the commission describes the dire impacts of prolonged cold exposure on Ukrainian civilians, saying that the country’s medical authorities documented deaths caused by low temperatures in homes, and even in hospitals. “Medical personnel from hospitals reported that during the past winter, they attended to patients who developed cold-related trauma, including various degrees of frostbite and hypothermia. The patients had developed these conditions at home, due to exposure to unheated premises and required hospitalization,” the report said. The report quotes a civilian woman living in Dnipro, Ukraine’s fourth largest city, who describes the impact the Russian attacks had on her. “Cold—it paralyzes you; there’s simply no way to get warm, and terrifying thoughts come into your mind,” she said. Blaming Putin and others The UN commission report names several high-profile Russian officials as the people most responsible for what it describes as “war crimes and the crimes against humanity.” It says Russian President Vladimir Putin made several “statements concerning instructions to commit attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.” It also alleges that evidence collected over the past few years shows that Russia’s former Minister of Defence Sergei Shoigu and his successor Andrey Belousov, as well the Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov, have been responsible for planning and overseeing attacks. The International Criminal Court has previously issued arrest warrants against Putin, Shoigu and Gerasimov for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. As the colder weather begins to arrive in Ukraine, Russia has made it clear it intends to continue to terrorize its neighbor The report mentions a declaration made by the Russian Ministry of Defence in August, which announced attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and said: “In winter you will freeze.” Ukraine is increasingly struggling to defend itself against these large-scale attacks because of a critical shortage of air defense missiles. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has made repeated pleas with Kyiv’s western allies for more ammunition, specifically pointing to the upcoming winter as a major worry. Kyiv had been targeting Russian oil and gas infrastructure, in efforts to hurt the Kremlin’s revenues from energy exports. However, it has eased these attacks after criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for rising gas prices. “Human trafficking” The report released on Monday also investigated Russia’s methods of recruiting foreign nationals to serve in its armed forces, concluding they amount to human rights violations and trafficking. CNN has reported extensively on Russia’s use of deception, bribery and blackmail to lure foreigners into joining its military. People from multiple countries in Africa, India and Latin America have described being promised jobs in Russia only to find themselves on the frontlines. The commission said it found “compelling evidence” that Russian authorities, working with agents, have “trafficked persons from 29 countries, using deception or coercion, to recruit them in the Russian armed forces.” It said the fact that Russia has used the same tactics to recruit people from multiple countries “demonstrates a high degree of coordination between agents operating around the world and the Russian authorities.“ “Promised payments and bonuses were usually diverted by recruiting agents and military commanders, passports and phones were often confiscated, and contacts between agents and families were interrupted, once the recruits were deployed to the front.” The report concludes that Russia violated the recruits’ fundamental human rights, including the rights to life, freedom, health, and to be treated humanely. The commission also investigated Ukraine’s recruitment of foreign nationals into its army and said that testimonies it collected showed that those joining the Ukrainian armed forces “did so knowingly and voluntarily,” understood the contracts they were signing and received salaries.

articles.title: Trump says Norway ‘sucks’ after Nobel loss
articles.summary: President Trump declared on Sunday that Norway “sucks” after he was not selected to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. The Norway-based selection committee honored Navi Pillay, a former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge, instead. “I said to our great first lady, ‘First lady, I get the Nobel Prize in two weeks, and it’ll be an…
articles.body:
President Trump declared on Sunday that Norway “sucks” after he was not selected to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. The Norway-based selection committee honored Navi Pillay, a former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge, instead.

“I said to our great first lady, ‘First lady, I get the Nobel Prize in two weeks, and it’ll be an honor,’” Trump said while rallying in Michigan . “You know, I feel much better about saving all those lives. How about India and Pakistan? I stopped them from fighting. They shot down 11 planes.”

“The prime minister of Pakistan said, ‘President Trump has saved at least 30 million lives.’ So I said, ‘First lady, first lady, it’ll be a great honor to get the Nobel Peace Prize next week when they announce it,’ and then I sort of forgot about it because I am busy,” he continued. “And it was announced, and it was gotten by a woman that nobody ever heard of.”

“I said, ‘What about me? Do they do two of them?’ Think of it. I settled, so I’m not in love with Norway,” the president stated. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a s—house country, actually.”

“Now it’s crazy what’s going on out there. It’s called the world of politics,” he concluded.

The president has openly coveted the award . Last year’s prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, presented the award to him in Washington.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee, which is responsible for selecting each year’s peace prize recipient, clarified that Machado’s gift to Trump was not an official transfer of her award to him.

Trump stated earlier this month his belief that he “should have won” the Nobel Peace Prize, adding in a Truth Social post that “no one ever heard of [Pillay] other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel.”

The Norwegian Nobel Committee selected Pillay this year for her work “in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted,” the committee wrote in a press release .

In addition to her time on the ICC, Pillay served as a United Nations high commissioner for human rights and was the first nonwhite woman in South Africa to establish her own law practice. She recently chaired a U.N. commission that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza .

articles.title: Iran’s anti-negotiation hardliners turn against President Pezeshkian
articles.summary: Iran’s anti-negotiation hardliners turn against President Pezeshkian over negotiations with the US.
articles.body:
As the threat of a new war with the United States looms, the Front of Islamic Revolution Stability, a hardline political faction also known as the Paydari Front, has asked the Iranian parliament and the Supreme National Security Council to initiate a withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

This move has been interpreted as a call for Iran to develop nuclear weapons, with the Paydari Front saying these military endeavours should happen “as quickly as possible”.

It is the latest bold and defiant message by Iran’s hardliners against Washington, after the US and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28 on the pretext that Tehran was trying to develop nuclear weapons.

The war has seen the Strait of Hormuz largely closed to shipping, massive damage to Iranian and Arab infrastructure in missile and air strikes, and huge disruptions to global energy supplies.

The past eight months have also marked an ongoing existential power struggle between moderates and centrists, such as President Masoud Pezeshkian, who generally favour talks with the US, and hardliners in the Paydari Front who do not.

Ultimately, the moderate camp wants a swift end to the conflict to save Iran’s crumbling economy. Hardliners believe Washington only understands the language of force, so the war should continue until the US capitulates to Iran’s demands .

The domestic rivalry can be seen in the public squares of major Iranian cities, where for the past 200 days supporters of the hardline faction have rallied at night.

Initially, these gatherings were a way for people to express public support for the government and protest the unprovoked US war on Iran. Over time, they have evolved into highly organised political rallies where activists can publicly express their strong opposition to moderates’ efforts to end the war through diplomatic channels.

The hardliners’ slogans include “No compromise, no surrender – the fight against America” and “Negotiating with the enemy is a betrayal of the homeland”.

They also protested against President Pezeshkian’s return to Tehran from the UN General Assembly in September , where he condemned the US war but also extolled the virtues of diplomacy . The pickets were viewed as a way for their “anti-negotiation” message to be heard by the president.

This bloc has considerable power beyond these activist circles. Hardliners have a strong presence in Tehran’s municipal government, the parliament, among religious preachers and eulogists, and academia and the media.

Amirhossein Sabeti, a member of parliament aligned with the Paydari Front, said in a statement that negotiations with the US will not begin unless Washington’s siege on Iran’s southern ports or sanctions end.

“The enemy’s objective of destroying Iran has not changed. It is simply waiting for the right moment to launch another surprise attack. Those who thought negotiations could prevent war, or that the United States would lift sanctions through negotiations, did not understand how the world works and were deluding themselves,” he said. “The only language the world understands is the language of power.”

The political faction to which Sabeti belongs has filed a motion in the Iranian parliament to impeach Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, following his visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. Iran’s parliament is also considering a law to criminalise interviews with foreign media outlets, which would be another win for hardliners.

But as the impeachment motion against Iran’s foreign minister moves through parliament, the political camp supporting the government continues to advocate for a diplomatic solution to the current conflict.

Davood Heshmati, a journalist considered close to Pezeshkian, said there are signs that US forces have foregone the grand ambition of overthrowing the Iranian government and have instead opted for more modest aims, which makes a diplomatic solution more likely.

“There are several ways to achieve those other goals, one of which is war. But, in any case, to prevent a war, all alternatives to military action must first be tested. Negotiations and a diplomatic agreement are among those alternatives, and they should always take precedence over war,” Heshmati told Al Jazeera.

“Those who say the Strait of Hormuz must not be reopened are people who believe the war must not end. From the perspective of Iran’s anti-negotiation camp, the war between Iran and the United States has no end. What they do not explain is what outcome they expect from this war. They seem to believe that, after several rounds of fighting, the United States will simply walk away from the conflict. But that idea does not appear to be consistent with the logic of what we are witnessing.”

He indicated that for any war to end, there needs to be an understanding with the US that respects Iran’s territorial integrity.

“Those in Iran who support negotiations argue that a balance of power does not necessarily have to be achieved through war, although, given everything that has happened along the diplomatic path, the distrust that exists is understandable,” he said.

Political analyst Negar Mortazavi argues that hardline groups are a powerful domestic force, but they currently have limited influence over Iran’s foreign policy.

“Iran’s hardliners are not a marginal political force. They are a well-organised and deeply entrenched part of [Iran’s] political establishment. Their strength lies in their ability to mobilise supporters, shape political discourse, pressure the government, and raise the political cost of diplomacy,” she said.

“But political influence should not be confused with ultimate decision-making authority. Decisions about war, peace, and negotiations are made at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and national security establishment.”

Hardliners can continue to confront negotiators, threaten impeachments against those who propose talks with the US, and try to obstruct diplomatic endeavours, she said. But they cannot prevent an agreement being reached if it is backed by the country’s main powerholders, including Supreme Leader Mujtaba Khamenei and the Supreme National Security Council.

“The [hardliners] are powerful enough to complicate diplomacy, but not necessarily powerful enough to stop it. [They] are a highly visible and vocal political force, but they are not calling the shots,” Mortazavi told Al Jazeera.

“Throughout the war, Tehran has kept the door open to diplomacy, and the decision at the highest levels of leadership has been to pursue negotiations with the United States and seek an agreement. The hardliners have been unable to stop that. The real test of their power is that they could not stop the JCPOA [nuclear agreement] under [former President Barack] Obama, and they could not stop the more recent MoU [memorandum of understanding] with Trump. Ultimately, the decisions were made above their heads.”

Street rallies and television programmes opposing a peaceful solution to the US-Israeli war against Iran will continue. But the delay in scheduling the foreign minister’s impeachment hearing, alongside continued diplomatic engagement with mediators to end the war, suggests that the moderates are still a force to be reckoned with.

articles.title: Trump predicts Canada trade dispute will be resolved ‘soon’
articles.summary: President Trump said Sunday his trade war with Canada will be over “soon,” as the dispute poses ongoing political problems for Republicans in the midterms. During a rally in Port Huron, Mich., Trump reiterated his view that Canada “has been ripping off” the U.S. “for years.” The president used that justification in imposing 50 percent…
articles.body:
President Trump said Sunday his trade war with Canada will be over “soon,” as the dispute poses ongoing political problems for Republicans in the midterms.

During a rally in Port Huron, Mich., Trump reiterated his view that Canada “has been ripping off” the U.S. “for years.”

The president used that justification in imposing 50 percent tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of goods from Canada in August. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched those levies “dollar for dollar,” with no public signs of a deal between the two sides.

“I had to do it. We’ll have that settled pretty soon,” the president said Sunday, referring to the trade war .

Trump also claimed Canadian officials “are willing to give us anything” as part of a trade agreement.

The Hill has reached out to Carney’s office for comment.

The president has threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian imported cars, trucks, auto parts and steel from 25 percent to 50 percent on New Year’s Day.

Carney, meanwhile, has responded to the trade war by deepening his country’s alliances with Europe and seeking less dependence on the U.S.

Multiple Republicans in difficult election battles have pushed back against Trump’s tariffs, including former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), who is running for Senate in the Wolverine State.

Rogers said Sunday on NBC’s “ Meet the Press ” that the auto tariffs concern him “a little bit,” as his state relies heavily on the industry.

“We’re going to go back and work through those issues to get some relief to make sure that it’s good for Michigan,” he told host Kristen Welker.

The White House on Friday exempted paperboard cartons, plastic boxes, refrigeration equipment and other products from the levies, a decision praised by Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is in a tough reelection fight.

“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” said Collins , who is in a close race with Democrat Troy Jackson.

articles.title: Students flag policy gaps, demand JEE Advanced third attempt
articles.summary: Student-led campaign urges Education Ministry and JAB to allow a third JEE Advanced attempt, citing CBSE attendance rules, dummy school crackdown and prep constraints.
articles.body: New Delhi: A student-led campaign seeking a third attempt at the Joint Entrance Examination (JEE) Advanced has urged the ministry of education and Joint Admission Board (JAB) to revisit the eligibility criteria, arguing that the current policy does not adequately account for the demands of regular schooling following the crackdown on dummy schools.The JEE Advanced Third Attempt Movement has linked its demand to Central Board of Secondary Education’s (CBSE) enforcement of the 75% attendance requirement and action against dummy schools. The group argued that students are now expected to balance regular classroom attendance with preparation for one of the country’s most competitive entrance examinations, while being restricted to two attempts in two consecutive years, including the year of their Class XII examination.According to the movement, complying with attendance requirements can make it difficult for students to devote sufficient time to JEE Advanced preparation, particularly for those without access to intensive coaching. It contended that allowing a third attempt would effectively give candidates two full years to prepare after completing school.The group also highlighted the difference in eligibility windows between JEE Main and JEE Advanced. While JEE Main allows candidates to appear over three consecutive years with two sessions annually, JEE Advanced offers a significantly narrower opportunity window, it said.The movement argued that the current two-attempt limit leaves little room for candidates affected by circumstances such as medical emergencies, accidents or disruptions during preparation. articles.title: Russell Brand asked assistant for female fan phone numbers, court hears
articles.summary: Helen Berger said she left her job working for Brand after she became "sick of him."
articles.body:
A former personal assistant of Russell Brand has told a court she was instructed to get phone numbers for the entertainer from female fans when she first started working with him.

Helen Berger, who worked closely with Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, said the request "felt uncomfortable" and, after seeking advice, she told the TV personality that she would not do that anymore.

Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

Brand had an "insane sexual appetite", Berger told Southwark Crown Court in a written statement on Monday.

Berger left her job with Brand after she became "sick of him", she said. She added that he had sex with numerous women during the time she was his assistant.

She described a work environment where Brand would ask her if he could "go and have sex now" when frustrated with a particular task.

Berger added that she never "witnessed anything against the law" but that "everyone normalised and dismissed his behaviour" so it "made me think it was accepted."

She told the court that "peacock" Brand found random women online to satisfy his "insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night", but sex often made him depressed.

She told the court Brand used MySpace to find women for sex, and said: "At his house, women often came over and it was clear they were there for sex."

She recalled once finding a female celebrity asleep in Brand's bed while he was wandering around the house half-dressed, and said of the comedian: "He was like a peacock, women would always approach him."

Russell Brand's defence team says any sexual activity was consensual and accounts have been twisted in the light of a defamatory TV documentary in 2023 which made allegations of sexual abuse against the entertainer.

The prosecution is due to finish on Tuesday morning.
